title: India Moves to Ban Fake Paneer as States Crack Down on Dairy Fraud
excerpt: FSSAI plans to outright prohibit analogue paneer while Maharashtra has already imposed a one-year state-wide ban, with 35% of tested samples failing safety standards.
body:
• FSSAI's Central Advisory Committee has finalized a proposal to ban analogue paneer outright, phasing out roughly 1,000 existing licence holders
  • Maharashtra imposed an immediate one-year state-wide ban on manufacture, storage, and sale of artificial paneer in August 2026
  • Out of 308 paneer samples tested in Maharashtra between April 2025 and March 2026, 109 (35.4%) failed state standards — 30 were declared unsafe
  • Madhya Pradesh is simultaneously expanding dairy infrastructure, aiming to become India's top milk producer with new cooperative societies and processing plants

A Crackdown on Fake Paneer

India's food safety regulators are moving to eliminate analogue paneer — a cheap substitute made with vegetable oils, starches, and emulsifiers that mimics the look, feel, and taste of genuine dairy paneer but lacks its nutritional value.

The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has finalized a proposal through its Central Advisory Committee to ban analogue paneer entirely, according to officials and documents reviewed by Mint. The decision, formally adopted in March 2026, would phase out manufacturing by roughly 1,000 current licence holders.

"A decision on selecting analogue or paneer cannot be left to the discretion of the consumer, considering the awareness level," FSSAI's internal document states. "Hence, it is suggested that the restriction may be made regarding the manufacturing and selling of any dairy analogue products."

Maharashtra Acts First

Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration moved ahead of the national regulator, imposing an immediate one-year state-wide ban on analogue paneer in early August 2026. The gazette notification bans processing, packing, wholesale, retail, and serving of non-dairy paneer variants across all districts.

Hotels, restaurants, caterers, cloud kitchens, and local eateries are explicitly forbidden from using or serving analogue paneer. Serving it in place of genuine dairy paneer has been designated an unfair trade practice, according to IANS.

The data driving the decision is stark: of 308 paneer and dairy analogue samples analyzed in Maharashtra between April 2025 and March 2026, 109 samples — 35.4% — failed state standards. Seventy-nine were sub-standard, and 30 were declared outright unsafe.

"It's like allowing gold-polished brass or aluminium jewellery to use the BIS hallmark logo."

— R.S. Sodhi, Former Managing Director, Amul

Why It Matters for Consumers

Paneer is a dietary staple and primary protein source for hundreds of millions of vegetarian Indians. While branded dairy paneer from Amul or Mother Dairy retails at around ₹460 per kilogram, unbranded loose paneer — often analogue — sells for as little as ₹250-300 per kg. About 90% of paneer sold in India comes through this price-sensitive loose market, making fraud easy and detection difficult.

FSSAI is deploying two scientific tools to identify fake paneer: fatty acid profiling and the beta-sitosterol test. Beta-sitosterol, a plant sterol found in vegetable oils but virtually absent in pure milk fat, has a regulatory threshold of 7 parts per million. Anything above that is a red flag.

"Consuming such products does not give the benefits that the customer expects. Long-term consumption is unhealthy not only because of the fats but also the emulsifiers that can disrupt healthy gut bacteria," said Dr. Rajeev Jayadevan, a public health expert and former president of the Indian Medical Association, Cochin, according to Mint.

Madhya Pradesh Pushes Dairy Expansion

While regulators eliminate fakes, states like Madhya Pradesh are simultaneously building out legitimate dairy infrastructure. Chief Minister Mohan Yadav has announced plans to make MP India's top milk producer — it currently ranks third — through the formation of 1,752 new dairy cooperative societies, modernization of the Gwalior dairy plant, revival of the Shivpuri dairy unit, and development of a milk powder plant in Indore with a capacity of 3 lakh litres.

Sales of Sanchi dairy products, including ghee, paneer, and buttermilk, have grown sharply, with ghee sales rising nearly 17%, according to state officials.

What's Next

The national ban, once finalized, would give existing manufacturers a transition period to remove analogue products from the market. The move has drawn support from major dairy players including Mother Dairy and the Indian Dairy Association.

"This decision is a seminal moment for the food industry at large. It goes beyond one product category and presents an opportunity for the industry to collectively raise benchmarks," said Shashi Kumar, founder of Bengaluru-based Akshayakalpa Organic, according to Mint.

Legitimate non-dairy alternatives — tofu, soy-based products, and coconut cream — remain available and are explicitly distinguished from the prohibited analogues under existing regulations.
nri_angle: Affects the quality of paneer available across India, a staple food for the Indian diaspora visiting or sending for family back home.
author: Diaspora Desk
